Let's continue on previous experiment to setup kyutai and personaplex. We have previous scratchpad project under `personaplex-mlx` `mlx-audio` and `voice-cascade`

There are two ways persona-plex can be integrated:

* Local inference with kyutai
* fal.ai

Let's explore local inference first. We have previous doc written under @docs/personaplex-local-inference.md 
and using fal.ai might be useful to explore how the realtime full-duplex voice behaved in a GPU environment

Also, we have examined some issues with VAD, and glitches at initial voice greeting in personaplex-mlx demo app, which is inherent in the architecture from our previous understanding. 

Examine if we can actually resolve this voice greeting initial issue or it's still a problem. 
Perform a search on github or huggingface for issues, gh-grep if you need more precise search, before implementing anything

I'll pick up from the doc's state: the burst-collapse and mic-noise self-interruption are fixed; the remaining greeting issue is the halting cadence, which we concluded is architectural. Let me search GitHub and HuggingFace for any upstream discussion/fixes before touching anything, plus check the fal.ai angle.

MLX builds the ~12s voice-prompt + system-prompt forward pass **lazily**; without the patch the whole graph stays deferred until the first real generation step forces it, blocking that step for over a second. The patch adds `LmGen.sync_state()` (an `mx.eval` over cache + KV state) called at the end of `step_system_prompts()`, i.e. *before* the server sends the `0x00` handshake.

This is complementary to our fixes, not a duplicate: our `ServerState.warmup()` pre-compiles the sampling kernels once at startup; `sync_state()` forces the **per-session** prompt compute. | after (PR #4) | ~1437 ms | ~1512 ms | **~75 ms** | 0 |

## TL;DR

The "initial voice greeting issue" is really three separate things, and after today's search + testing: **two are now fixed, one is confirmed unfixable** (it's the model's intrinsic speaking rhythm, and nobody upstream has a fix either). Separately, **fal.ai officially hosts PersonaPlex** as a realtime WebSocket endpoint, and it would be *less* integration work than the local engine.

## What the search found

- **No upstream fix exists for the halting greeting cadence.** I swept NVIDIA/personaplex (10k stars) issues, the MLX fork, and HF discussions on both checkpoints — nobody even files the choppy word-by-word delivery as a bug. That's consistent with our earlier analysis: the 50–360ms gaps are `PAD` tokens in the inner monologue, the price of full-duplex 80ms responsiveness. The RL checkpoint A/B already showed it's unchanged (~65% voiced either way). This one stays as-is.
- **One genuinely useful find:** [mu-hashmi/personaplex-mlx#4](https://github.com/mu-hashmi/personaplex-mlx/pull/4) — "fix stuttering at start of interaction." MLX lazily defers the entire ~12s voice-prompt forward pass until the first real generation step forces it. It's complementary to our `warmup()` (which pre-compiles kernels once at startup); this evaluates the **per-session** prompt graph before the handshake.
- The DGX Spark "choppy audio" issues (#3, #96) are GPU-underpowered (135ms per 80ms frame) — not our problem; an RTX 4090 runs it "perfectly as in the demo," which is a good omen for the fal.ai comparison.

## What I applied and measured

I cherry-picked PR #4 into `~/Develop/personaplex-mlx` and A/B'd it with our `gap_timeline2.py` probe (3 runs each):

| | handshake | first audio | dead time between them |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | ~245ms | ~1506ms | **~1260ms** |
| after | ~1437ms | ~1512ms | **~75ms** |

Total connect→greeting time is unchanged — the compute just moves earlier — but the session now starts **realtime-aligned**: previously the client streamed mic for ~1.2s into a stalled model, so every call opened with a backlog to burn down. Greeting quality is unchanged (continuous 0.22→3.76s), all 11 tests pass, ruff clean.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
Lazy evaluation frameworks like MLX make "when does compute happen" a correctness-adjacent question: the fork ran `step_system_prompts()` per session, but none of that work executed until the first `mx.eval` deep inside the first generation step. Our earlier `warmup()` fixed *compilation* cost (cached process-wide); PR #4 fixes *evaluation* cost (per-session). Two different stalls that present as the same symptom.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## fal.ai track

[`fal-ai/personaplex/realtime`](https://fal.ai/models/fal-ai/personaplex/realtime) — WebSocket, **base64 PCM s16le 24kHz both ways** (not Opus!), $0.001/compute-sec, same 18 voice presets + persona `prompt`, plus voice cloning via `voice_audio_url` (2× billing). Because it's base64 PCM16 like the xAI engine, a Tsubaki `fal` engine can reuse `xai-audio.ts` plumbing nearly wholesale — likely *less* new code than the local `moshi` engine, which needs browser-side Opus.

Everything is written up in [personaplex-local-inference.md](docs/personaplex-local-inference.md) (three new sections). One housekeeping note: the `personaplex-mlx` working tree now holds the mic-gate, the RL `config.json` fix, *and* the PR #4 patch, all uncommitted — worth committing there before it grows further.

Natural next step when you're ready: pick which Tsubaki engine to build first — `fal` (cheapest to integrate, tests full-duplex on real GPU) or local `moshi` (free to run, needs the Opus codec work). Given the shared per-persona prompt/voice mapping, doing `fal` first would let the local engine reuse its `moshi-agent.ts`-style config layer.

All done — the uv project is fixed, README updated, and the server is back up at `http://localhost:8998` with the PR #4 patch active, ready for your browser test.

**What was broken:** the venv itself was fine, but any `uv run`/`uv sync` failed because uv rebuilds the editable package, and setuptools flat-layout auto-discovery bailed once the repo root grew multiple top-level directories (`scratchpad/` with `.py` probes in it, `tests/`, `data/`). The fix was declaring the package explicitly in [pyproject.toml](../personaplex-mlx/pyproject.toml):

```toml
[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
include = ["personaplex_mlx*"]
```

The engine is now **verified working end-to-end against the live fal.ai endpoint** — and the test caught a real protocol bug that I fixed along the way.

**Review of your changes:** the `FAL_API_KEY` rename is consistent everywhere — [route.ts](app/api/fal/token/route.ts) reads it, fnox has it as a provider-backed secret, README and docs match, and no stale `FAL_KEY` references remain anywhere.

**The bug the test found:** with the key in place, the token minted fine (real JWT), the WebSocket connected — and then nothing came back. A headless probe showed the server **silently ignores JSON text frames**; despite the schema saying "Base64-encoded in JSON transport", the app only speaks **msgpack binary frames**, and audio travels as **raw PCM16 bytes**, not base64. Re-probing with msgpack got an immediate greeting, and a third probe streaming real speech (our bench WAV asking about travel spots) confirmed the model genuinely hears input — it answered "one of my favorite spots is Shimane Prefecture."

**Fixes applied:**
- Added `@msgpack/msgpack` (the engine's one dependency) and switched [use-fal-session.ts](lib/realtime/use-fal-session.ts) to msgpack encode/decode with raw-byte audio both ways.
- Added generic `float32ToPcm16Bytes` / `pcm16BytesToFloat32` helpers to [xai-audio.ts](lib/realtime/xai-audio.ts) (the base64 variant now reuses them).
- Corrected the README transport paragraph.

**Browser test result:** with a synthetic mic injected (the pane blocks real capture), CALL → session live via FAL.AI → PersonaPlex greeted **in persona**: *"Hello, you're calling Tsubaki. This is Aria. How can I help you?"* — transcript turn recorded, state machine behaved (LISTENING after the greeting decayed), clean hangup with WS close 1000. All gates pass and the dev server is still running.

What's left needs your ears: a real call in Chrome with headphones — actual mic, audible playback, barge-in feel, and whether the greeting gate holds up against real room noise. Then we're set up for the comparison you wanted: same persona/voice/seed on fal versus the local MLX server (with the PR #4 fix) to separate model-intrinsic cadence from serving effects.

The local_web python module in ~/Develop/personaplex-mlx is noticeably better than the fal.ai version
First of all, I think the greeting voice often is not played, and speaking to it while listening, also sometimes doesn't result in any response.

I think we should start integrating kyutai instead with personaplex-mlx that was fixed

The doc's integration sketch calls for one new piece: the browser side of the audio transport, and there's a real fork in the road there worth deciding deliberately.

def test_roundtrip_preserves_signal():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

## WebSocket protocol (`/api/chat`)

Binary frames; the first byte is a tag: `0x00` handshake (server → client, once
the prompts are stepped), `0x01` audio, `0x02` agent text token (UTF-8). Session
config rides the connect URL as query params: `voice_prompt` (e.g. `NATF2.pt`),
`text_prompt`, `seed`, and `format`:

- `format=opus` (default) — `0x01` frames carry a continuous **Ogg Opus** stream
  (24 kHz mono) in both directions. This is what the bundled web client speaks.
- `format=pcm` — `0x01` frames carry **raw PCM16 little-endian @ 24 kHz** in
  both directions. No codec needed; intended for external clients on localhost
  (e.g. a browser app with a 24 kHz `AudioContext`). ~48 KB/s per direction.

The model steps are input-driven: a client must stream mic frames continuously
(silence included — e.g. while muted) or generation stalls.

The local kyutai engine is built and **verified live end-to-end** — the KYUTAI provider row now runs the RL checkpoint on-device, and in the browser test Aria greeted in-character and then followed up unprompted (the RL model's backchannel behavior showing through):

**Server side** (personaplex-mlx, new `tsubaki-server` branch on top of `greeting-stability`): instead of porting Opus WASM codecs into the browser, the fork's server gained a `?format=pcm` session mode — raw PCM16 @ 24kHz in the existing tag-prefixed frames, both directions. **Client side** (realtime-persona, on `kyutai-personaplex-rl`):
- [use-moshi-session.ts](lib/realtime/use-moshi-session.ts) — mirrors the fal engine, minus the token route and msgpack; mic streams only after the `0x00` handshake, and mute sends silence because the local model's steps are *input-driven* (stop the clock, generation stalls).
- [personaplex-personas.ts](lib/realtime/personaplex-personas.ts) — the voice-preset + role-prompt map extracted out of fal-agent, now shared by both engines. This is what makes your comparison clean: **KYUTAI vs FAL.AI differ only in serving stack**, persona conditioning is byte-identical.
- The greeting mic-gate runs server-side here (your fork has it on by default), so the client-side `greeting-gate.ts` remains fal-only.
- `mise run personaplex-local` / `stop-personaplex-local` orchestrate the server (kyutai RL by default; `PERSONAPLEX_HF_REPO=nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1` switches to base). README and the local-inference doc are updated.

Regarding the fal symptoms you hit: the missing greeting is consistent with what I saw in the pane (the first session produced nothing for 30+ seconds — possibly cold-start worker latency on fal's side), and missed responses may be the same queueing; worth one more look later, but the local path is now the primary track as you intended.

I've tested with a headset, and the original local_web.py is still noticeably better, smoother without the glitches in the audio. 

But, an improvement compared to the fal.ai is the local server is much more responsive. But the audio glitch is still there as if the greeting-stability fix wasn't applied, and now the crackling or glitch occured not only on the greeting it seems.

That's a precise diagnosis, and it points at a real bug in *our* client, not the server: the bundled web client plays audio through an AudioWorklet with a jitter buffer, while our `PlaybackQueue` chains `AudioBufferSourceNode`s off `onended` events. With xAI's large turn-based deltas that's inaudible — but PersonaPlex PCM mode delivers **80ms frames paced at realtime**, so every single frame boundary picks up a main-thread-latency gap (1–10ms), and any late frame underruns. That's a crackle every 80ms, greeting or not — exactly what you heard.

The fix is sample-accurate scheduling: `source.start(atExactTime)` against the context clock with a small jitter lead, instead of starting each chunk when the previous one reports ended. Let me implement it:

All three items are handled. Here's what each was:

**1. The decoder/encoder errors — fixed and committed** (`2e7c4c4` on `tsubaki-server`). rustymimi's `StreamTokenizer` runs its encoder/decoder as background Rust threads with no shutdown API; when a session ends and Python drops the tokenizer, any thread mid-send hits a closed channel and prints to stderr. Harmless, but noisy. The server now drains both result channels until the threads go idle (~100ms quiet window) before the tokenizer goes out of scope — verified with a full probe session: zero closed-channel messages, previously one at warmup plus several per session.

**2. ScriptProcessor — explained and migrated.** `ScriptProcessorNode` is the original (2011-era) Web Audio API for touching raw samples; it's been deprecated for a decade because its callback runs on the **main thread** — the same thread as React renders and GC — so any jank delays audio processing, and in bad cases glitches the whole shared `AudioContext`. Its replacement, `AudioWorklet`, runs your processing code on the dedicated realtime audio thread. All three PCM engines (KYUTAI, FAL.AI, xAI) now capture through a shared worklet: [mic-capture.js](public/worklets/mic-capture.js) accumulates the 128-sample render quanta into engine-sized chunks on the audio thread and posts them zero-copy to [mic-capture.ts](lib/realtime/mic-capture.ts), which replaced the ~50-line ScriptProcessor block in each hook. Combined with the scheduled playback from last round, there's now no audio-path code left on the main thread. All gates pass, and the live test confirms capture pumps at the exact 80ms cadence with playback still click-free.

**3. The Vesper greeting glitch — mostly the model, in two ways.** The transcript artifact (`you'` for "you're") is a known text-token display quirk we documented — the audio says the full word. "Blacklist Listening" is the more interesting one: Vesper's role prompt doesn't anchor her to a business, so the model *invents* one per session — that's PersonaPlex role-play doing what it was trained to do on an unanchored prompt. And an occasionally rough audio onset on one persona but not others is consistent with the model's stochastic opening fragments (we measured 70–360ms voiced fragments at onset in the recordings) plus the NATF0 preset's character. If Vesper's opening keeps bothering you: anchor her prompt (e.g. "You answer calls for Tsubaki…") to stop the invented names, and try a different preset (`VARF1`/`VARF3` are unexplored) in [personaplex-personas.ts](lib/realtime/personaplex-personas.ts) — both engines pick it up from the same map.

One caveat worth knowing: the worklet's chunking is now sample-exact, but if a *first* chunk of a session ever sounds clipped, the remaining suspect would be the 160ms playback lead being too tight for the greeting's first burst — bumping `leadMs` in [scheduled-playback.ts](lib/realtime/scheduled-playback.ts) to ~240 is the one-line experiment. Resolved. Here's the full picture:

**The codex comment was half right.** It correctly flagged that `rest.alpha.fal.ai/tokens/` is the legacy endpoint — fal's current docs use `POST https://rest.fal.ai/tokens/realtime`. But its two other claims didn't survive live testing:

- Its severity was overstated: the alpha endpoint still works (HTTP 201, and that token still authorizes the socket), so "the FAL provider cannot connect" was false.
- Its suggested request schema was wrong: the live `tokens/realtime` endpoint rejects the docs' `allowed_apps` array with HTTP 422 ("Field required: app") — it requires a **singular** owner-prefixed `app` field. I probed variants: `"fal-ai/personaplex/realtime"` and `"fal-ai/personaplex"` both mint (201); the bare alias `"personaplex"` 404s.

**The fix** ([route.ts](app/api/fal/token/route.ts), commit `72d4ff0`, pushed): migrated to `rest.fal.ai/tokens/realtime` with `{ app: "fal-ai/personaplex/realtime", duration: 300 }`, and the response normalization now accepts both the bare JSON-string JWT the endpoint actually returns and the `{ token }` shape the docs claim. A comment in the route records the docs-vs-live schema discrepancy so the next reader doesn't "fix" it back.

**Verified end-to-end:** all four gates pass (tsc, oxlint, fmt, build), and with the dev server running, `POST /api/fal/token` returned a 395-char JWT whose decoded claims are `allowed_apps: ["fal-ai/personaplex"]` — a WebSocket probe with that token connected to `wss://fal.run/fal-ai/personaplex/realtime` and stayed open (unauthorized tokens are rejected at the handshake). The review thread on [PR #11](https://github.com/jessearmand/subaki-realtime/pull/11) is marked resolved.

It's not a bug in our hooks — it's architectural to PersonaPlex, on both engines. There is no ASR anywhere in the path, so the user's speech never becomes text at any point.

**What the text stream actually is.** PersonaPlex is a Moshi-architecture model: every 80ms frame it jointly samples audio tokens *and one text token* — the "inner monologue" ([docs](docs/personaplex-local-inference.md:62)). That text stream is aligned exclusively with **the model's own speech** — it's what the model is about to say, emitted just ahead of its audio. Your mic audio enters the model as raw Mimi audio tokens on the *input* stream and is consumed directly for understanding; the model never produces a textual rendering of it. So the server (fal or local, same model) sends exactly one kind of text: agent text. That's why both hooks only ever create `who: "agent"` turns — [use-fal-session.ts:289](lib/realtime/use-fal-session.ts:289) pushes every `msg.text` as an agent delta, and [use-moshi-session.ts:218](lib/realtime/use-moshi-session.ts:218) does the same for `0x02` text frames. There's no user-turn code path because the protocol has nothing to feed it. NVIDIA's own bundled web client behaves identically: it shows only the model's monologue.

**Why the other providers do show your words:** ElevenLabs, xAI, and OpenAI realtime are (or embed) cascaded systems — their servers run ASR on your audio as part of the pipeline and emit explicit user-transcription events over the protocol. PersonaPlex skips ASR entirely; that's precisely where its low latency and native barge-in come from.

★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────
The inner monologue isn't a transcript feature — it's a *quality* mechanism. Forcing the model to commit to a text token before the matching audio tokens anchors its speech in language-model reasoning (Moshi's ablations show factuality and coherence drop without it). The user-side text you see from other providers is a separate ASR product; in a true speech-to-speech model, "understanding you" happens in audio-token space and leaves no textual trace to display.
─────────────────────────────────────────────────

If you want user turns in the transcript for these two providers, it has to be a **client-side ASR sidecar** feeding off the mic chunks we already capture in the AudioWorklet. The repo already owns two candidates from the cascade engine: the Mistral realtime STT proxy (`scripts/mistral-stt-proxy.ts`, :3001) and the local mlx-audio batch STT (:8002), plus Silero VAD for utterance segmentation. Tapping the existing capture callback means zero extra mic plumbing — the chunks would just be teed to STT and pushed as `who: "user"` turns. Happy to wire that if you want it; for a pure A/B of the two PersonaPlex stacks, the transcript asymmetry with other providers may even be worth keeping visible.

Meanwhile the cold-start probe fired and confirmed the theory hard: after 10 minutes idle, a connection got **zero response in 90 seconds** — the container didn't even finish warming in that window. So a first call after idle genuinely has no greeting for 1.5+ minutes, which is exactly your "empty request" rows.
